marsh, Lauenborg and Oldenborg, Make Known: On the report of our Minister of Finance who has laid before Us the deliberation of the Colonial Council on a Draft of an Ordinance to extend to the Danish Westiudia Possessions the Law of 29th December 1857, enacting that funds belonging to minors shall, in future, when not exceeding 100 Rdl., not be given in trust to the Upperguardians, &c. We do most graciously decree :

The Law of the, 29th December 1857 enacting that funds belonging to minors shall, in future, when not exceeding 100 Rdl., not be given in trust to the Upperguardians, etc. is hereby, and in the following manner, extended to the Danish Westindia Possessions, with such modifications as circumstances peculiar to these islands, make necessary. $ 1.

From the first day of July 1860 minors' funds not exceeding 100 dollars are not to be given in trust to the Upperguardians, unless the minor in question should already possess in the trust of the Upperguardians a larger amount to which they can be added; whereas such funds are to be paid over to the guardian of the minor, who, in so far as they are not required for the necessary use of the minor shall be bound to have said funds placed out at interest on good security, and in due time, the minor becoming of age, to account to him or her for the same.

% 2- The funds in trust of the Upperguardians on the 1st day of July 1860, and not exceeding 8100, are gradually to be paid out ; the guardians of minors, however, for two years from said date, not having the right to exact payment of such amounts, whereas the Upperguardians shall be authorized during this period to pay out said funds, whenever such payment is rendered possible by new funds being given in trust to them, or by outstanding funds being paid after legal notice; in which case the guardians are to receive due notice, three months previously. To which all concerned have to conform.

COMMUNICATION. A FEW QUE ST I ON S Is it true, that the Burgher Council intend again to petition Government for leave to employ the accumulated funds of the Country Treasury on loans to individual planters on Bureau Accouuts : Is it true, that the grant or refusal to applicants for these loans depends not upon the degree of certaiuty to the Treasury against eventual losses, but on the contrary on the difficulty of the applicants in obtaining credit in other quarters 1 Is it true, that in order to satisfy the demands for loans from the Country Treasury on interest at the rate of 6 per cent, the Burgher Council not only borrowed money from the Bunks on discount at the rate of 9 per cent, but that the difference between the two rates is permanently charged on the Country Treasury, as has been asserted in the Avis without meeting contradiction ? Is it true, that of the $35,000 or thereabouts thus lent out last year, 20,000 were lent to members of the Burgher Council as has also been publicly asserted r Is it true, that it has been discovered, that the accumulations of the Country Treasury cannot legally be applied to extraordinary measures of vital importance to the Colony, f. i. t he introduction of foreign labourers, but that in the face of a large cxistiug surplus fund the necessary supplies must be procured by new taxes ! Has any thing been done on the part of the Burgher Council to obtain a remedy from the legislature against the glaring defect thus alleged to have been discoveied ?

Is it true, that while new severe taxes are being laid to a great extent on unproductive and comparatively valu< 1 ss land (or the expressed purpose of furthering one particular measure of public utility, the capability of the Treasury to meet these expences is being curtailed at the recommendation of the Burgher Council by the abolition of other taxes existing from time immemorial, on the plea of the Hour ishing condition of the Treasury ? Is it true, that any one who in the most moderate terms questions the propriety of the doings here alluded to, is to ipso an enemy to the country, and that such conduct admits of no other explanation, can have no other motive than malevolence ? Finally and principally, is it to be expected, as long as the funds of the island are permited to be loaned out (either at. 6 or at 10 per cent) on the recommendation of those who more or less arc the borrowers, that they will be used for the most necessary and indispensable of all extraordinary purposes of general utility, immigration ?

The above was written before the Avis of 5th inst. came to hand, containing two advertisements from the Chairman of the Burgher Council, the one calling on planters to apply for the loans, " in like manner, as last year," the other advertising for the delivery of 600 puncheons Cora-meal. From this it must be inferied, that the measure is not only adopted by the Burgher Council but sanctioned by the Governor.

SCIENCE AND ARTS. Mr. Faraday's lecture on pharoology, or the science of light-houses, has attracted attention on both sides t lie Channel, seeing that it treated of the magneto-electric light, which is superior to all oilier electric lights hitherto invented. For six months past, an experimental light ot this description has been displayed at the North Foreland, whence it sends its beam far into France, and as Mr Faraday shewed by aid of a cloud of steam, pierces a fog in which an ordinary light would he totally invisible. Hence the magneto-electric is the very light for the fickle atmosphere of coasts ; but there are questions of cost and mechanical arrangement to be settled before it can be generally adopted. A company in France þÿ L'Alliance þÿ state that they have overcome the question of cost aud of mechanism, and are seeking for a method of producing carbon cylinders which shall be at once homogeneous and good conductors; which, having accomplished, they will be ready to treat with the imperial government for the establishment of the magneto-electric light in the lighthouses of F ranee. Signor Parvesi of Turin makes known another application of charcoal likely to be u-eful in pharmacy. Dealers in drugs know that castoroil, if kept, too long, will turn rancid ; the remedy is to mix it with animal charcoal and a smalt quantity of calcined magnesia, and keep it for three days in a temperature of from sixty-eight to seventy-eight degrees, when the oil on filtering off is fiuud to he in all respects better than

tin- best of the freshly-made. þÿ Dr Anselmier has presented a paper to the Academy of Sciences at Paris on what he calls Artificial Autopbagy þÿ that is, a way by which mariners and others, wlieu deprivod of food, may keep themselves alive for a long time by opening a vein, and drinking small quantities of their own blood at p riodical intervals; which seems something nke applying the theory of perpetual motion as a preventive ol starvation. Professor JDu Hois Keymond of Berlin, pursuing his researches in physiological chemistry, shews that the acid which is said to be generated in living muscle is in reality a result of death, not of vital action ; and further, that the fluid which appears as acid on a transverse section of the muscle, is found to be alealine when the section is longitudinal. þÿ Dr Tbeophilus Thompson, whose paper on the effect of cod-liver oil in multiplying the red corpuscles of the blood, we noticed last year, has lately made a communication to the Modicochirurgical Society, on the medical administration of ozonised oils. The mode of preparation is to saturate the oils used iu medicine þÿ sunflower, eodliver, if c þÿ with oxygen gas, and expose them for some daysto the directaction of sunlight, when they may be used as a remedy consumption. for Their effect is remarkable ; the rapidity of the pulse is reduced, and by thus bringing back the circulation to its normal condition, an important advantage is gained over the malady, and the general health is improved. þÿ M. Houzcau, pro-

fessor of chemistry at Rouen, has set up a series of delicate instruments to test the air, and is able therewith to note the indications of atmospheric deterioration, and some of the phenomena that accompany epidemics. We hear, moreover, that he professes to extract the ozone from the pure air of the country, and carry it into the town, to renovate the atmosphere of factories and hospitals. þÿ M. Paul Broca, a surgeon of Paris , has repeated the experiments made and described some time ago by Dr Braid of Manchester, as hypnotism; in other words, catalepsy without inhalation. One result of the repetition is, that he finds hypnotism as effectual as chloroform in deadening sensation during surgical operations, having tried it in some very servere cases. It appears that the physiologists of France have only become aware of Dr Braid's experiments within the past few months: and M. Broca intends to devote himself to study all the possible applications of hypnotism as an anaesthetic agent. Meteorologists are collecting observations on our unusually backward spring, to compare with the records of past years, us a further help in examination of the question as to the weather-

cycle theory. The same atmospheric condition appears to have prevailed over the whole of Europe, accompanied in several parts of the continent by combined thunder and snow storms. Of these the most remarkable occurred in Belgium on February 19, between seven and eight in the evening, when, besides an unprecedented fall ot snow, twelve churches weie simultaneously struck by lightning, at places wide apait þÿ Liege, Courtrai, Malines, Antwerp þÿ comprising neurly the whole breadth of the country. Some of the churches were completely destroyed, and the others more or less injured. þÿ Chambers's Journal.

A New Sedative. þÿ The Journal de Chimie Medicate contains the following remarkable account of the discovery of a powerful sedative in cases of neuralgia by Dr. Field : þÿ Some time ago that gentleman was induced by a homoeopath to put two drops of a solution, supposed to he diluted to the first degree, on his tongue, in order to try its effect. After the lapse of about three minutes he felt a sensation of constriction at the base of the neck, then violent singing in the ear, while his forehead became covered with abundant perspiration. He then was seized with uncontrollable fits of yawning, and lemained senseless for several minutes ; his head fell back, his lower jaw sank down powerless, he became extremely pale, and for two minutes his pulse was silent. The homoeopath, perceiving ihese symptoms, was terrified, thinking he bad unconsciously committed a murder. Stimulauts, however, brought Dr. Field to consciousness again, but he contiuued to feel a headache for half-anhour after, with a sensation of pressure at the epigastrium, and general weakness These symptoms disappeared in the course of that time. It was evident that the substance employed was a powerful poison, and that it had not been sufficiently diluted ; and it turned out to be nitrate of oxyde of glycile, a substance obtained by treating glycerine at a low temperature with sulphuric or nitric acid. One drop, mixed with 99 drops of spirits of wine, constitutes the first dilution. Dr. Field was immediately struck with the idea that he had

experienced the t fleets of what, in a much weaker dose, must he a useful sedative of the nervous system, while the homoeopath was overjoyed at having discovered what be conceived to be a powerful remedy lor apoplexy. After various trials upon animals Dr. Field at length resolved to test this tew remidy on patients. He did so first on a lady 68 years of age, who had long been suffering from neuralgia, which returned at intervals of three hour.-, and had resisted every remedy known, such as ammonia, a.-safoetida, chloroform, Ac The fourth part of a drop of the above solution being administered, she was at once relieved, but some of the symptoms experienced by Dr. Field being felt by her also she discontinued the remedy, but her sufferings soon obliged ber to have recourse to it again, and she was completely cured. It has since been tried in casesof headache and dental neuralgia with equal su cccss. þÿ Galignani's Messenger.

MORE ABOUT THE PRIZE-FIGHT. The Journal des Debats has devoted four or five of its columns to a description of the late fight between Heenau and Sayers. As the narrative is almost entirely taken from accounts that have been already published in English newspapers it would tie superfluous to reproduce it. But the following conclusions of the writer ! of the article are not devoid of interest : þÿ þÿ This struggle, then, brought face to face tho Old World and the New þÿ Old England and Young America. The American giant, is tall and strong, like the trees of the New World; his frame is iu proportion to the forests, the lakes, and the rivers of America; lie reminds us of primeval nature, of the men who measured seven cubits in height, as in the early ages of the world. Face to face with him we have seen the Old World, the product of the ages | that have passed away þÿ the highest expression and pruduet of civilisation þÿ the creature of art. And yet, after all, these two athletes are of the same blood, sprung from the same stock. It was England in its youth and England in its manhood, but the race was the same. These two men were rivals, but they could not be enemies. They might accost each other, as the Homeric heroes were wont to accost each other, and to engage, as theyr did, in single combat. But woe to the stranger who should meddle with them, for, surety, iu such a case would their united strength be turned against the meddler! The Englishman, looking at the American as lie recoiled from his blows, could

not but think with pride, þÿ It is I who have done this þÿthing; and yet he was also proud of the blows he received from the giant of tbo New World, for therein lie could not fail to recognise the vigour of the race. What we in wish to point out is that the Englishman this struggle appeal s as the faithful type of his nation. What are the attributes of the English race? What but endurance, patience and energy, often latent, but always fierce, and that never kuows deteat þÿ an obstinacy that will not be to yield? Even conquered, and a in secret oath to die rather than the story ot this fight wo find one and all of those attributes. Even at the ri-k of offending the delicate tasti s of our readers, we will say that in the sternly obstinate and inflexible resolution witli which the Englishman, apparently unconscious of the pain in his right arm, supported, with one arm only, and that the left, the shock of the terrific avalanche which fell upon him, is, in our eyes, a triumph of moral force, and a miraculous exhibition of will. Five and twenty times was he flung upon the sward, and five and twenty times be rose again, the living image of England on the field r t battle. History tells us that Englishmen are men of strong character, they gather always beaten in the first campaign force ; like all from misfortune. It seems that, like Animus, they | must ki-s the earth before they know their strength, for, after a series of defeats, we find tin m ever masters of the field of battle. If they

are not thoroughly beaten at first, their destruction will be a work of lime. But there is still another reason which has made us allude to this singular fight. Wc mean the profound, and universal, and ardent interest which it has aroused in England, and which seems to us to have a political significance. During the last year and a h Jf Volunteer Rifle Corps have been foimed in England and the newly-awakened popular interest in the recent fight is intimately connected with the prevalent idea among Eng 1 i sh men of the necessity of taking measur, s for the defence of their teriitory. Several of tho French newspapers, in speaking of this light, have only seen in it a rude and disgusting ex hibition. For our-selves we recognise the play of animal instinct, but we think that there is something else to which attention should be paid. The first defence of England consists in her wooden walls ; but her second line of defence consists in the broad chests and formidable arms which pla\ t heir part in contests like (hat we have described England sees in them a provision tor the d fence of the country. Such, it seems to us, is tho moral of this fight þÿ such the explanation of the interest it has excited in every class of English society þÿ and such is our excuse lor having occupied the attention of oar readers witli a description of þÿit

M Craven, of the slave bark Wildfire and her cargo of 520 negroes, and the arrival and disembarkation of the latter upon Whitehead Point, near Fort Taylor. Key West, May 13, 1860. The United States steamer Wyandotte, Lieutenant Commanding Fabius Stauley, arrived at this place last night from the south side of tho island of Cuba, having in custody the bark William, of Baltimore, with five hundred and sixty African negroes on hoard The Willi was direct from Africa, and was about lull mg her cargo oi humanity when stie was pounced upon by the little steamer Wyandotte and her gallant crew. The negroes are all young, but greatly emaciated by their inhuman treatment and close confinement during the voyage from Africa. This is the second capture made within a very short space of time, and they certainly speak well for the little United States steamers Wyandotte and Mohawk and theirgallant crows When the þÿWilliam s cargo shall have been landed at Key West, the United States Marshal will have over one thousand Africans under his care. The hark William exhausts her supply of food to day aud will probably discharge her cargo, at the African depot to-morrow. She lias been in communication with the land, and had on board a Spanish custom house official at tho time of capture. The quarters just finished for the cargo of the Wildfire will possible house this new accession by close stowage, but there is a want of lumber for further extension, as well as a sup-

ply of provisions. If this new impetus towards the suppression of tho trade shall be increased by the proposed bounty of $ 100 per head, we may look for other captures, and it will then become a matter of policy and humanity to hive the slaves afforded every convenience and comfort for health, preparatory to Laving for their return voyage. 'This is a matter that requires immediate attention by the government. CHRISTIAN3TED, ST. CROIX. TUESDAY, 10th APRIL, 1SG0 After a pretty severe drought, the weather has, at length, become more favourable. On Sunday and on the followii g day, many heavy showers of rain fell on the western portion of this Island. In our town, we have had but a small share of this rain, not more than two or three lines having fallen, although at the time we write we have every appearance of rain. Tho roads we observed on a tour over the Island, are not in as fine a condition as ihey were formerly kept. On the way to West End we saw a large number of cocoa-nut branches strewed acro.-s the road ; an occurrence, which we are aware not unfrequently, in former days, led to the infliction of fines. On our way up from West End we were a witness to an example of unwarrantable and outrageous conduct, which we would not intrude on the notice of our readers, except as a warning against the repetition of similar conduct. Our carriage, at a short distance from West-End, was hailed by an individual in another carriage. Anxious to know who had hailed us, and suspecting that that individual was one from a party of pleasure which we had just left, we enquired, þÿ Who are þÿyou? The individual drove past, and halted at a short distance in front of us, and on our coming up, he slashed with his carriage-whip across the front of our carriage, in punishment, as bo said, for our having asked þÿ Who are þÿyou? He inflicted two lashes on our companion, and on our making known who we were, and enquiring the cause of his unprovoked assault, he attempted to justify his con-
duct and refused to make an apology. Capt.

$j tr ® P; 8i ft li 4 Hi 0 ® McGregor, who received the lashes, on identifying the perpetrator o! the act as the manager of tile Estate þÿBetty Hope, s Mr. Knight, declined iuflicing summary punishment on him ; but, we belu vi , pr fers to bring an action at law for this uu warrantable attack on the public roads.

( London Weekly Dispatch , March 11 ) The state of Europe embraces tbe not unequal chances of coming war or cuntinuid peace The event may involve Great Britain in its most s, lions consequences In any case, all that we are building up of commercial and industrial extension, all that we are venturing in reducing the sources of revenue to win the gains of an enlightened policy, all that we are anticipating in war reswui ces by applying the income-tax to peace provisions, are parts of a brave speculation which depends upon tranquillity for its success; peace not only between ourselves and other nations, but such peace as shall at least preserve us from their jealousies, I and from all complications, fears, and doubts j which may cripple our own transactions. It will not, be wondered at, then, that, as journalists, we should deem it our duty to take the most comprehensive view at the present condition of Continental politics. And we declare at once that we have even a grander and a heat tier interest than that of British wealth in tbe mighty contention between þÿman s freedom and his þÿdespots will, which we see going on around us. But could we limit our regards to the narrowest, selfishness, we should yet be obliged to say that the true liberties of mankind, their value, their use, the responsibility to claim them, and act with conscience as their possessors being once made known, as it now is to all the civilised populations of the earth, it is quite impossible that any inferior interests can find sure ground to stand upon

until tho rights of the nations and of the human race are settled in this all-determining battle. So, without further excuse for a lengthened summary, to the central point, the fate of Italy. The discussion between M. Thuuvenel on the part of France, and M. Favour on behalf of Italian unity and independence, has come to an issue. A- yet, the terms are stated with calmness and consideration; but the determination tii.it lies beneath the words is, at least on the' one side, stern, and, if opposed, threatening. M. Thouvcncl, onr readers know, has proposed and that Victor to Emmanuel Parma Modena his dominions in full shall antrex sovereignty, and that the Romagna shall be held by bim as a Vicariate under the Pope. Tuscany is, according to the French policy, to keep its þÿ autonomy, its s pirate existence, as a State. Whom Napoleon would make its Sovereign dots not appear, or whether he would defer in that altogether to the choice of the Tuscans. And M. Thouvenel says, in plain terms, that the annexation of all Central Italy to Sardinia would indicate an arriere pensen which would threaten war against Austria fir the liberation of the Venetians, and would place the Pope and the King of Naples in danger of having their dominions ul.-o absorbed in the Italian kingdom. Count Favour's answer is very mild in language, veiy decided in substance, lie tells M. Tbouvenol that the offer now made, and to which France pledges full support, that she will be þÿ behind and with þÿSardinia in its ac-

complishment, might have been readily, if not enthusiastically, accepted immediately after the peace of Villafranca ; that Piedmont, on its own part, may accept it now; but that, with regard to the Italians of the Centre, it is an impossibility. The teiterated promises of Napoleon that no intervention by force shall hold down the popular will have given the populations, whose destinies are to be decided, the full impression of their own right in the matter. This light is recognised thoroughly by the Piedmontese nation as sealed by the Emperor, and if any Ministry were to dispute or thwart it, the Parliament of Turin would speedily cast that Government aside; if Victor Emmanuel himself were to refuse a second time the offer which would tend to perfect his own patriotic work, lie would thenceforth only reign by force, a tyrant, not a popular Sovereign, a mere monarch opposed by all the hopes of selfregenerating Italy. Cavour then dares all that M Thouvenel suggests that, Piedmont w ill risk in taking hor own course independently

of French patronage. He will brave all who impugn the Italian choice. He will submit, by suggestion to the governors, a question to the universal suffrage of the people of Parma and Modena, þÿ Independent government, or annexation to þÿSardinia. He expects the same question to he put in as unequivocal terms in Tuscany. In the Romagna he will not suggest tbe þÿ þÿVicariate as an alternative, for he says that the people there will have no Government in which the Pope may be expected to interfere, and that the Pope himself would probably rather part with the rule altogether. Victor Emmanuel giving him the honours of suzerainete, paying him a valuable tribute, and even pledging himself to support the Papal throne in arms, to which conditions M. Cavour is ready to subscribe. To use a very homely English proverb, but the most expressive one. for the purpose, wbat M. Cavour will not do is to play the game under the condition for bis adversaries, þÿ Heads I win, tails you þÿlose. He accepts beforehand the decision of the peoples by universal suffrage given under the secre y of the Ballot, lie will forward frankly to the populations all that M. Thouvenel thinks fit to put forth by way of argument to influence their decision. But if M. Cavour will tike þÿ no to the annexation as definitive, and will in that ease give the utmost help of Piedmont to the formation of the independent Governments chosen in Central Italy, lie will be equally bound by the þÿ yes which signifies annexation to Piedmont, and will then

defend tbe United Kingdom, comprising all ihe States that vote themselves numbers of it, even at that, very fearful ribk which M. Thouvenel points out to him, and which he ueither denies nor extenuates. Let us remark here that the pledge of Piedmont to defend the Papacy is an honourable safeguard against further revolution in Italy. It is an indirect guarantee for the safety of the Neapolitan dyuasty. It will be well for those who dread the great, united, poweiful, free Italy, which is the hope of the enthusiastic, the generous, and, as we think, the wise and foreseeing, to accept this stop in the career of the unification they tremble at. If they reject it, they take the hazards of the future. It maybe that Sardinia risks all, a frightful amount of physical suffering, a yet more awlnl danger of moral annihilation, by accepting and asserting the union with Central Italy. It may be that Victor Emmanuel and his noble fellows in arms may lose and perish, be entombed in devastation, amid fire and blood. But it is also possible that they may win, all the more so from the despeiation of the stake, if they are forced to throw for it, and then, Italy will be one ami free from the Alps to the seas Count Cavour offers a middle term, which the politician who rcjecis it may live but a few months to regret having relused. FRIDAY, 13tii APRIL, 1SG0. þÿ þÿ On Tuesday last a bottle was picked up on the sea-side adjacent to the Estate Granard, by the proprietor of the Estate, Mr. Hope, which, on being broken, was found to contain a number of British Postage-stamps of different values, and two small coins of the East- India Company (two two-anna pieces) joined together by a ring, as a shirt-button. The coins were perfectly bright, but lite postage-stamps were almost illegible. The bottle, apparently, had been for some time in the sea, as barnacles had attached themselves to the cork There is no clue to determine whether the bottle was thrown overboard by some person on the point of shipwreck, or whether, as has often been done, it was merely intended to throw further light on the direction of Ocean Currents.

It will appear very improbable to some of our readers that a vessel, on her voyage from this Island to St. Thomas, should experience any other distress than that which the weather may effect; yet such appears to be the case. The schooner Rosaline, on her voyage to St. Thomas on Monday last, with about twenty passengers on hoard, got out of provisions and water ; and but for the providential circumstance of their being some cocoa-nuts and other fruits on board, intended to be sold in St. Thomas, the passengers must have suffered a great deal more than they did. This is no uncommon occurrence however. We know many instances where, in the face of a certainty of having a long passage, the captains of these Schooners have provided food and drink to last hut for a few hours.

London Times March lo. Either the llapshurgs are selling off or a most impudent hoax is in progress. We find an advertisement in the columns of a contemporary announcing that an English auctioneer has received instructions to sell on the 20th proximo a " valuable and important collection of "ancient arms and weapons of war from

t T\ < ft 6; ll ft ft Vv M , " Hungary." It is announced that these were obtained at the disarming of Hungary, and were purchased by the present proprietor, a gentleman of Liverpool, from the Austrian Government. The collection, we are told, is very complete, for it consists of many thousand stands of arms, and contains everything in the shape of a weapon which could be found in the country. Here we have the spear for the Hungarian national standard, with the famous date of 1848, the lialhert-heads and spear-heads used by the " liberty weapons," insurgent peasantry, and what are called no doubt implements of the rough-and-ready sort. The disarmament must have been very complete, for we find in the list even Court swords with fine rapier blades, and handles carved and worked in gold and silver, þÿ surely rather acmes de luxe than weapons dangerous to tyrants. The duelling pistols in proper hands might have done service, but surely the " an- " cient match and wheel locks, inlaid " with ivory and mother-o'-pearl, with " Albanian barrels beautifully inlaid with "gold," could scarcely have inflicted much damage on the Tyro lose Jsigers. Modern science has contrived, too, to draw the teeth of the "ancient forms " of ordnance," but the Austrian agents seem to have been of opinion that they could not without danger to Caesar be left in the possession of Hungarian Oldbucks. Antique Styrian rifles, conteaux de chasse, with ancient blades, dated 1279, Albanian scimitars, blunderbusses, fowling-pieces, þÿ everything, in short, in

the shape of a weapon which could be found in Hungary, has been seized by the Austrian Government, and in due course sold to VV. .1. Grazebrook, E q.. of Liverpool. This is to hang the carpets out of the windows of the Burg Palace with a witness! The process is gone !" It would painfully suggestive be of " Going, difficult to cite any going, parallel case in history to this instance of prudent forethought. Whoever < omes after the llapsburgs will find nothing but bare walls. The family is busy "realizing." It might be as well to look about us, and see if we could not come to an understanding about the pictures in the Belvedere, and buy the wild beasts at Sehbnbrunn for the Zoological-gardens. The Austrian auction will make a noise in the world. We can but regret that the only auctioneer who could be supposed equal to the occasion has passed away front this earthly scene without having enjoyed such an opportunity for the exercise of his peculiar talents. What an advertisement Mr. George Robins would have drawn up with such a theme before him as the selling off' of the Austrian monarchy! With what unction he would have introduced the crown of St. Stephen to the notice of a discerning public, and Maria Theresa's chemise de nuit, and old Francis's cotton nightcap ! There is a shrewd, homely common sense, about the proceeding which would have warmly commended it to the favourable acceptance of the illustrious Empress and Emperor last named. How differently they manage these things in France!

There a King is turned about his business between a sardine and a cup of coffee, clapped into a brougham with the terse direction to the coachman " Au large!" and the next minute the Parisian mob are in the Royal apartments pulling the knickknacks about, and dancing the cancan in the Throne-room. Obviously nothing of this sort will take place at Vienna. Cnesar is taking Time by the forelock, and disposing of his goods and

chattels in time. He will make a very different end of it from that silly fellow Sardaiiapalus, who could find nothing better to do with bis property than to set fire to it, and looked on while the devouring element raged ' with irresistible fury," and caught now a sofa, and now a King. Our prudent young friend at Vienna, should any untoward event occur, will leave no ashes behind hint but cigar ashes. This Austrian auction is a notable event. Among monarchs, indeed, we cannot recall a precedent of a solemn "selling oft';" but some few years back we had something of the same sort among ourselves, when the Duke of Buckingham's affairs went wrong, and Stowe was brought to the hammer. The ruin ofa Duke excited considerable interest, but what is that in comparison with such a tact as the Emperor of Austria's little embarrassments? It is, indeed, painfully evident that he must be "hard up" before he would have had recourse to such an unintperial expedient as selling off his curious and ancient armour to a foreign speculator. By a strange twist in the human mind these useless articles are just the very last things that a gentleman in difficulties can make up his mind to part with. See how readily a man will dispose of an estate, but how he will cling to a pair of < Innese mandarins, a collection of Turkish mouthpieces, or a cage of stuffed amadavads. There is another curious feature in this case. Were these arms the property of convicted rebels, confiscated to the use of

the Crown with all legal ceremonies, or were they simply seized as a measure of precaution? Upon the latter supposition it would seem scarcely right to dispose of them bj absolute sale, unless, indeed, there is an intention of" handling over the proceeds of the transaction to the owners of the arms. The mere suireestion c r» of ativ such intention J will seem ridiculous enough to as many of our readers as have any knowledge of Austrian dealings with Hungary for the last ten years. The young Emsweep of that unhappy country as peror's agents have made as clean if a was possible for men to do who have been trained from their youth upwards in the science of making clean sweeps. It seems a pity, while the Emperor Francis Joseph is selling off his collection of armour, that our own collectors should not endeavour to come to terms with the embarrassed Sovereign for the contents of the Amhras Museum. We remember in former days to have seen there various suits and articles of ancient armour which would prove valuable additions to our own collection in the Tower of London. There is in especial a suit originally made for Alexander Farnese, Duke of Fa rut a, for which, if we could arrange matters quietly with Ctesar. liberal posed to deal on we should he dis- terms. Then we remember something of the helmet of Francis I. of France, of the suits of Don John of Austria and Philip II. of Spain, of the tomahawk of Montezuma, Emperor of Mexico, and of a suit of armour which belonged to Charles V.,

which we should be sorry to see pass into other hands than our own, if Francis Joseph carries out his idea of selling off' the old Hapshurg stock in trade. He would, no doubt, he able to realize a, very considerable sum for the mere contents of the Ambras Museum. The Imperial Library would also fetch a good price. The Emperor, too, is rich

in curiosities. We doubt not tliat the present proprietor of Madame Tussami's Exhibition would make a fair offer for tile crown with the false stones, the sceptre, and the robes worn by the First Napoleon at his coronation in Mil anas King of Lombardy. Besides, as the present French Emperor is engaged in making a Napoleonic collection in the Louvre, he wo ild, no doubt, be glad of the cradle of the young King of Rome, better known, perhaps, as the Duke de Reichstadt. The proceeds of the sale, as one should imagine, would be very large if the young Emperor could manage to include in it the regalia and the chains and collars belonging to the dresses of the various Austrian orders worn by bis ancestors. He is, perhaps, adopting the wisest course in not throwing all his curiosities into the market at once. At least, by this new arrangement be will have introduced an entirely new feature into the fiscal system at Vienna. The Emperor himself will have contributed to the necessities of the State. þÿ that is, if to State purposes are applied the proceeds of the Austrian auction.

The 3d Crown member, Stakemann, expres sed his intention to vote against the purchase of Bulowsminde for which no motive of recommendation wiis contained, either in the draft, or the Report of the Committee, except the personal comfort of the Governor. He did not share the somewhat gloomy views of the state and future prospects of this island, expressed on many occasions during this session aud of which also the Report now uuder discussion bears evident traces. He attributed the falling off in the production of our staple. articles ever since emancipation in a great measure to merely temporary and transitory causes, in particular to errors in the system of conducting the Estates, such errors being t lie natural consequence of the sudden total overthrow of the previously i xisting relations of the agricultural labour, as also to the unfavorable state of the weather for several years. He saw a proof of the justice of this more encouraging view in the circumstance, that in the midst of the general diminution of the productions, which was not confined to the naturally less fertile Estates, some proprietors at least had carried on the business with considerable success, aud it was only natural to suppose, that their example would be followed by the rest of the planters. Notwithstanding this opinion he could not approve of the expenditure utider discussion, as not sufficiently supported by reasons of necessity or public utility. As far as the proposal of the Committee, amounting to a virtual aban-

donment of the existing Governmenthouse as a dwelling, he considered that even on the question of comfort to the Governor the measure would defeat its owu object especially if the latter should have a numerous family, and in cases of sickness, when a removal to town might sometimes be found advisable. lie must also add, that whatever effect the measure might have ou the comfort of the Governor, it would in his opinion not be without some inconvenience to many of the inhabitants, whose position although without means of conveyance qualified them to, and in some measure requires their participation of the hospitality of the Governor, if his residence was permanently removed to a distance of half an hours drive. FRANCE A co: respondent writes: þÿ ' A disagreeable consequence has already ensued to the French Government tor having put forward the princi- ' ple of choiee of nationality,' by communities. The province of Franche Coiute has been clamouring to become Swiss. There are some antecedent reasons for this. The proviuce I allude to is one of those most violent against the commercial treaty, and, for the first moment, most injured by it. Franebe Comte, and in all the territory adjacent to the Jura, the maitres de forge,' are or think they are, ruined ; and they extinguish their furnaces, discharge their workmen, and throw up their arms in disgust. Upon this came also a discussion with the central authority about railroad lines, and the local functionaries and proprietors conceived they had grievous cause to complain of the barefaced corruption of the Government ageuts. In the very midst of all this quarrelling they hear it declared that every man is free to choose his own master, and at once they exclaim þÿ ' Then let us be immediately annexed to Switzerland, and become free.' 1 happen to know this in all its details, from people on the spot, and the movement is really a strong one. Of course the polioe mani- troops will keep down any such improper aud festation of public feeling as that I allude to, but it is, nevertheless, an undeniable tact, and one that shows the mischievous results of such a policy as Louis Na, oleon's. THE ANNEXATION OF SAVOY AND NICE. The " Moniteur'' of Sunday says : þÿ " The treaty by which the King of Sardinia consents þÿ to the approval of the Chambers þÿ subject to the annexatton of Savoy and the district of Nice to France, was signed on Saturday, the 24th ult., at Turin. This annexation will he effected without any constraint on the wishes of the population. The two Governments will concert the best means of obtaining a manifestation of this wish. The King has transferred the neutralised portions of Savoy with the same conditions uuder which lie possessed them. The Emperor promises to come to an understanding on the question with the Powers who sigued the treaties of Vienna of 1815, and Switzeiland. The Sardinian subjects who are natives of Savoy will enjoy lor one year the privilege of claiming the maintenance of the Sardinian nationality. A mixed commission of French and Sardinian Commissioners will determine the future irontiers of the two countries." It is stated that the Swiss Federal Council has received two verbal communications from France aud Sardinia. The Government consequently gave orders for that long road to be strongly occupied by detachments of horse arid foot gendarmerie, and General de Goyon contributed some companies of French iufantry for the preservation of order in the same locality. These dispositions, however, had the effect of checking the demonstration, and some thousauds of promeuaders resorted to the Corso instead, where great numbers of them appeared with ti e innocent distinction of bunches of violets in their button-holes. The patrols of gendarmes, wh had orders to parade the Corso, took umbrage at this symbol, aud insisted upon the promenaders walking singly instead ol taking each other's arms. So strange a demand of course brought on, in some cases, unpleasaut rejoinders; and the gendarmes, unaccustomed to admit, of any reply to their high behests, proceeded to make some arrests upon the Piazza. Coloinia, which were resisted by the people as unjust and ai bitrary. The people took this

triumph, and the gendarmes skulked in universal hissing They lost no time off amidst making their complaint at. head-quarters, and a quaiter of an hour later a patrol of horse gendarmerie entered the Fiazza Colonna Irom the Piazza di Pietra, whilst a strong detachment ol' foot gen- in darmerie issued forth front the police-office the Monte Citorio Palace on the other side. DEMAltARA CHINESE EMIGRATION The fine ship Whirlwind, after a shoit passage of only 78 days six of which were passed þÿ at the Cape of Good Hope þÿ arrived here ou the 12th instant from China, with 377 immigrants, of whom 56 are females. His Excellency the Governor, Mrs. Wodehouse, the Honorable William Walker, and Mrs. Walker, and other ladies and gentlemen went on hoard to look at the new comers, the arrival of Chinese females being quite an epoch iu the history of the Colony. The people were all in excellent health, and appeared quite cheerful and contented. Not a death occurred on the passage, and it is not too much to say that this freedom from mortality, and the good condition of the immigrants must be attributed in a great measure, to the care and attention shewn to them by Captain Edghiil and those under him, and to the cleanliness and ventilation preserved in the ship. The married folks occupied the afterpait of the vessel, and were separated from the single men by a screen ; each couple had separate accommodation, so as to secure privacy, and at the same time the partitions dividing, what may he termed the berths, were scarcely five feet in height in order not to check the circulation of air. The centre and (ore-part of the ship were allotted the people from Hong-Kong, and those from Canton, the two being separated to prevent collision between them. About a dozen others occupied the long-boat the whole passage, as they were not on good terms with any of the

Hong-Kong or Cantou immigrants, but, before leaving the ship, the feeling of mutual distrmt seemed to have disappeared. Altogether, the cleanliness not only above hut between decks, the excellent arrangements and the health of the Edghiil. Mr. Austin, by people reflect the greatest last credit on Captain accounts, was husy preparing for other shipments, aud it is to be hoped that the same good fortune will attend them as has attended the first. þÿ Royal Gazette March 23.

His Excellency Governor SOHLEGEL, Knight ol Danncbroge and Danncbrogsmand, &c., &c., &c. May it please Your Excellency, Your resignation of the high and responsible office, which you have, for five years, held amongst us, and your approaching departure tor Europe afford the inhabitants of our island au appropriate opportunity of which we avail ourselves of expressing to you the feelings of respect and confidence which we have ever entertained towards Your Excellency during your j official connection with us. In so brief an expression of our sentiments as this must necessarily lie, it would be impracticable to review the public history of Your þÿExcellency s administration, or to dwell on particular events connected therewith, hut we feel convinced, that we but express the feeling of the whole community, when we sincerely acknowledge Your þÿExcellency s constant and unremitting exertions for the best interests of our island, lour Excellency came among-t us at a period when our prosperity bad already begun to wane, from causes over which the Executive could have no control, and which no purely colonial legislation could remedy. Protracted seasons of drought, paucity of labor, occasioned by the great decrease of our rural population subsequent to emancipation, and the consequent want of capital, had combined to create a depression, which is unhappily still extending itself, and which, we fear will continue to do so, until the only perceptible remedy be applied by the successful execution of the

Immigration-Scheme, commenced under the auspices of your administration. This unhappy state of things lias undoubtedly added very much to the usual difficulties ol the Executive and curtailed its opportunity for beneficial action ; Gut we yet deeply feel, that amid all our smuggles, the inhabitants have ever met with Your þÿExcellency most s earnest sympathy and interest, lor which we should \ now offer our heartfelt thanks. Socially þÿ the departure of yourself and Lady Scill.EOKi. will leave a blank amongst us, which will be difficult to fill. Your united undeviatiug courtesy and kindness to all ; your ever ready, prompt charity towards the needy, have wou for her as for you, our highest esteem, and | we cannot, better conclude this inadequate testimony of our leelings, and our reluctant fare- j well to you and to her, than by earnestly praying the Almighty Giver of all good for his choicest blessings on yon boih wherever and in whatever station your future sphere of duty may be cast. We are, with reiterated expressions of esteem and respect, Your þÿPixcellency s most obdt., humblo Servants, St. Croix, June 1860
His Excellency, after a short reference to the contents of the address and signatures attached, expressed his sincere pleasure and satisfac-

tion at the receipt of this testimony- of the approval and kind feelings of so many Gentlemen whose favorable opinion he highly valued, and his pleasure was increased by- the conviction that the address contained only what he felt, himself justly entitled to claim, namely, a deep and earnest desire on his part for the benefit of the colony. I here was one view he had taken in regard to these Islands which he wished to state on the pi esent occasion, namely þÿ the necessity of abandoning the old System of originating every progressive measure through the Government ; as he was of opinion that, if a permanent and beneficial change was to be expected, it could only he brought about by the inhabitants themselves relying more ou their own exertions in matters where the internal interests of the Golony were concerned, and thereby hearing the responsibility of their own acts. The Government of the Porte is, on its part, using every effort to form a numerous army, in order to prevent Servia and the Danubian provinces from escaping from its authority aud gaining their independence. This army is at

present concentrated on five points. The army of ltoumelia is divided into four corps, which occupy a vast extent of ground, from the Herzegovina to Bosnia. Tho second is more numerous, and guaids the frontier of Servia: its head-quarters are at Pristina. Tho third is composed of 30,000 tnen, and is concentrated on the Danube, near Widdin, with its reserve at S qiliia. The fourth is stationed between the Danube and the Black Sea, that is, between Silistria and Kostendji. The reserve is at Schumls. The Porte has collected 30,000 men in Thessaly, mostly Redifs, for the purpose of acting against the Greeks, in case of necessity.

annulment no fee is to be paid.

LONDON, Wednesday, May 30, 1860. We hope Europe is not ungiateful to the Emperor of the French lor his continual care to reassure her and make her comfortable. It is a pleasant thing to have not only a peaceful and candid, but also a considerate neighbour. At once to watch and to work is too great a strain upon the body and mind. They who built the Temple found it hard to wear their arms as well as wield their tools, and even the shepherd would like to unsling his long gun while he pursues his blatant wanderers. It is kind of the Emperor to set M. Fould to assure us that there is nothing to fear. We should do better to confide in him. We should not then be led away by the feeling of uneasiness which ' parties" are strenuously endeavouring to spread. We should then go to sleep each under his own fig tree, satisfied that the Emperor is too loyal a neighbour and too faithful an ally to menace the rights of others. His moderation in the past is a certain guarantee for the future. So M. Fould says in his speech to the citizens and husbandmen of Tarbes, and as M. Fould is a Minister of State and sneaks from authority surely we may all go to sleep in peace. Why should Prussia bo uneasy and Belgium apprehensive ? Why should Royal personages confide to each other secret fears and start to find them fame? Why should England be silently and, we may add, mournfully assuming an attitude of prcpatation for some tremendous effort? Why should all the populations that lie round France be at this moment suffering every evil of war except that one evil

of bloodshed? It is astonishing what trouble human beings take to make themselves unhappy. Listen to M. Fould and be compose I What if there be a kite in the air, þÿ he means no harm. Nestle, ye plump partridges, and ye birds of golden plumage; he is not hungry yet, he has not digested his last meal; those wide sweeps and rapid swoops are only piny, his morning exercise to keep his wings in acin n. Provoke not the mighty master by your unbelief. M. Fould reminds you that "the Emperor " has several times proclaimed that he only wishes to insure to France the rank which belongs "to her." How say you, Belgium ? llowsayyou, Prussia? Are you not satisfied with this ? It would seem that the phrase scarcely falls like oil upon your ruffled plumage. Probably you are not quite sure what that rank may be which Franoo believes to belong to her. Possibly you may not be able to measure the area of the just proportions of a Napollonic Empire. Some vain apprehensions may be haunting you that such words as these may not be inconsistent with a desire for Antwerp and a thought of the froutier of the Rhine. Be reassured; the Emperor's Minister appeals to his master's previous character, and bids you measure the loyalty of the future by the moderation of the past "Nemo repente fuit turpissimus " No man can become covetous all at once. If, indeed, he bad ever shown a desire for other people's possessions ; if be had ever used his army lor purposes other than those of benevolence and love; if be had

ever brok n up a big State or bullied a little State, or snatched a province from a humble friend, tben indeed you might have had some pretence for yonr insensate suspicions. We see now it is. These States are "led away by the "feeling of uneasiness which parties are stren- "nonsly endeavouring to spread." Somebody has bean whispering in their ear the infamous

$ Tj1 P; Ri 0; ll % (k Vj 11 $ « calumny, that "the Emperor of the Fiench "makes war like a conspirator." They have been insidiou-ly reminded how Aus'ria wis broken to pieces and Piedmont partitioned to the accompaniment of generous phrases and disinterested proclamations. By an illogical process of reasoning they are moved towards the conclusion that what happened to others may happen to them. Germans have naturully a smack of pedantry about them. We should not wonder if they have been thinking of .Eneas madly rushing to arms when he saw his neighbour's house on fire, and of those often quoted lines, þÿ " Turn vern manifesto fides, Danauinqne patescunt' " Insidise. Jain Dei pliobi dedit ampla ruinam, ' Vulcano " Ucalegon." superante, domus; jam proxitnus ardet If it be true that there he any uneasiness among these timorous Powers of Europe þÿ and we have admitted and argued upon the fact only because M. Fould and the "Moniteur" iD.-ist upon it þÿ it must be the result of some imperfect reasoning, such as we aud M. Fould have attempted to expose. less true, that these ' parties" have been insidi- It is scarcely to be believed, but it is nevertheously suggesting to the Belgian aud the Prussian Governments that this Emperor of the French, whose loyalty, alter the assuiances I e has given and the acts he has done, it would be a sbaine to doubt, is at this moment repeating in the Low Countries those preliminary matiteuvres which preceded the disruption of Lombardy and the partition of Piedmont. They as.-eit that

the French Government speaks with two voices. It is declared that the French Government has a special Department in Palis lor the fabrication of newspaper articles to he slipped into foreign newspapers. They do this great potentate the wrong of asserting that lie pursues a sys em kuown to our low-class publishers and puffing tradesmen, of hoaxing innocent editors by foisting upon them bits of pieietidt d news wherein there is always a concealed busins 6s pu pose that escapes the eye. We have had such tilings cut out and sent to us from time to time, with a history of the authorship, origin, and seciet process by which the trap waswoik'd Of course, we have always had too firm a confidence in the loyalty of the French Emperor to believe a word of all this. We know that he never speaks anonymously; but the test of the world are not so assured, and are discouraged accordingly. Furthermore, these " parties," whom M. Fould so properly denouuees, go so far as to pretend that agents are now traversing the manufacturing towns of Belgium, explaining to thewiokmen and masters how much better off they would be if they were not cribbed aud confined in that narrow kingdom, but were portion of one great empire ; and that several have already been kicked out of workshops when the men had discovered their object. The "Nord," we are told, lias already felt its way by a cautious article upon the Freueh frontier. It is said that the Paris press lias already received ins: ructions to assert

that the Belgians are discussing the question of annexation to France, and that the same impudent falsehood has been adroitly foisted upon some of our own English papers of the more obscure and incautious class by M. Fould's ' parties" said to he now going on, All these things are and then they proceed to show that this is in accordance with all former Imperial practice, and that the plan has been first to get up a fictitious discussion, then to argue upon that discussion, then to assert that the discussion has terminated in favour of the aunexeis, then to manifest Impeople, and theu perial sympathy for to the wishes ot an unanimous much an overwhelming array to the desired territory. These they describe to have been the invariable stages of the annexation disease. We think with M. Fould that there is no present danger of this disease going to any fatal lengths in Belgium unless it Rhould unhappily first seize upon and carry off Rhenish Prussia. Belgium and Prussia were vaccinated against it more than fifty years ago. A Belgian or a Prussian is as little likely to profess a desire to become a Frenchman as is a Kentislrman or a Yorkshireman, and there are guarantees which make those overlying coasts of Belgium rather different to the slopes of Chablais. We say those things entirely in corroboration of M. Fould. Of course, so long as the present Emperor rules we arc safe in his loyal word; but thrones and dynasties and human life are tho sport of time. If we could compound with Fate that this loyal

and amiable and contented Entperor could reign for ever, and always in his present mood, and that M Fould shc u d always interpret his policy, we might lay a.-ide our apprehensions; but, as it is, perhaps "people" will do as well, while implicitly confiding iri the French Emperor's loyalty, if they critically note the signs of the day and watch how the storm-gauge rises aud falls.

A year ago we were accustomed to say that liugland was the only European Power of importance possessed of a representative assembly, as understood in this country. The Legislative Body ol France is þÿ what we know. At Berlin, though the Government is just and the mcmbeis patriotic, yet the constitution of the monarchy is such that military organization must predominate and the police, he a too powerful institution. Belgium, Holland, and Sardinia were States of the smaller class, uuablo much to influence Europe in favour of free institutions. But within a few months the cause of " Parliamentarism,'' as it is termed across the Channel, has gained by the development of one of the States attached to it. Sardinia has shot up, if not exactly into a first-rate Power, at any rate into a kingdom sufficiently strong to beaid Austria and to inspire Fiance with ical or affect" d apprehensions. Some dozen large and historical Italian cities, with a great expanse of territory, have been added to the domains of King Victor Emmanuel. In Lombardy lie possesses tho richest country and the most thriving and industrious population South of the Alps. In Tuscany he has gained a quickwitted people and a city which gives him the great" st moral influence in Italy. By annexing the Romagna he has not only set himself up as an antagonist of the Papal pretensions, hut lie has secured a position on the Adriatic which may be useful in time. Then there is the reversion to a good deal which has

not yet been obtained It seems understood that the King i- to be the heir to those of his Italian brothers who remain þÿ to the Emperor of Austria, the Pope, and the King of Naples It is impossible to look upon such a State as the kingdom of Saidinia now forms as if it were merely a common Second-ra'e Power. It is a strong kingdom of 12 0. 0 00(> souls. Befoio we are many yeais older it may be a formidable Empire of 26,000,000 I' is now, for want of a better name, called "Sardinia; it may soon aspire, with justice, to the name of "Italy." The Parliament of this great aud increasing State is just now debating a most important matter Perhaps never has a Parliament been field for patriotic declatnati hi. It is whether occupied with a subject which gave so fine >v a province shall he sundered from the monarchy. þÿ whether the Royal House shall prove its do votion to the Italian cause by surrendering all which connects it with regions which are alien in blood and language. Like the British Parliament, the Assembly at Turin is debating on a French treaty The Emperor Napoleon may boast that he cultivates alike the aits of conquest and commerce, when his two nearest, neighbours and most intimate allies arc agitated by his plans. For many weeks we have been pondering over the hetrefits which he has in store for us, and at the end we cannot determine whether our Chancellor of the Exchequer is about to inauguiate a period of immense prosperity, or is diopping the substance of valuable revenue in pursuit of the shadow of

augmented trade. .similarly, the Sardinian Deputie- are in wofitl doubt whether they have ma le a splendid baigain, or have been fh ecod by the bland hut somewhat cavalier benefactor who stipulated for the ces ion of Savoy. The two debates have a good deal in common. In the fust place, there is no doubt that the Government will carry its propositions by a large majority. The Deputies are Italians, who care nothing about Savoy or Savoyards who have made up their minds that to be a Frenchman is to be a very fine thing. There can be little doubt that the recent transactions wruld never have been contemplated if the indifference of Piedmont to Savoy and of Savoy to Piedmont had not been complete. The material interests of the two provinces, it has been shown, are not connected. The Savoyards, speak French, go to Paris to make money when they leave their country, or send their homo. produce to French towns when they stay noth- at Tho Italians, on their side, care ing for the poor mountaineers, whom they con-

sider as stupid as their own marmots. And, even if Savoy had been a more valuable province, with a more gifted population, it is probable that Italy would have been equally willing to part with it. The " nationalities" on j the Continent do not at all tend to agglomeration They have nothing of the same spirit which makes Englishmen proud to see Canadians, or Australians, or Hindoos submit to the sceptre of their ruler. Even among the most educated a narrow provincialism obtains which carries us back to the time of Squire Western in this country. An English Tory, with bis hatred of Hanoverians and Scotchmen, does not widely differ from an Italian of the present day, who wants Italy to be not only independent, but sttudered from every other connexion. A peasant on the extremest bill in Sicily is more a countryman of tho King of Sardinia's subjects than a Savoyard is; and, while earnestly expecting the extension of Victor Etninauuel's doinaius southwards, they are, on the whole, iuditfereut to the lossol his semi-French, semi-Swiss territoiy, in the Alps But there is another reason why these debates should have but one termination The cession of Savoy is an accomplished fact ; the constitutional and international law of Europe is so much at variance on the matter of treaties that there would be endless complications but for the prudence of popular representatives It is considered, anil perhaps reasonably, that the act of a Sovereign is, as regards foreign countries, the act of his own State. Thus with

Savoy, it had been agreed between the Emperor and his ally that Savoy should be transferred, certain foims being gone through which were supposed to indicate the consent of the Savoyards. All this has been done, and Savoy is now French territory. It may be ihat Victor Emmanuel is accountable to his own subjects, and that Cavour might be impeaeli» d as a traitor to the monarchy. But the powerful ruler who has got what lie wants need not trouble himself about any Parliamenta y anger The tiling is done, and even were Savov and Nice essential to Italian safety tocy c oild not be recovered. It is a principle in human naluie to bo cont nt with what is, and not even a Continental Assembly will push its rights so lar as to protest against that which is low beyond its coot i ol. We, who have opposed, so far as protests can oppose, the annexation of Savoy, are not likely to take any very great interest in the debates of the Tutin Parliament. The extension of French territory is a European question. It may lie said to concern Prussia, or Bivaria, or even England, much more than any Italian State. The countries on tho Rhine have s.un thing to lose by the precedent of 1860, and the question of Savoy is uot lor Piedmont, but for Europe. It is not a matter of Sardinian sentim. nt, but of European safety. The transfer of a little province may be of no moment in itself, but the example set by sueli facility of conquest may tend to the future disturbance of peace. But the Sardinians ate wise in leaving

all that to their neighbours, and in recognizing that the complications which the ces-ion of Savoy may bring forth ate for Powers of greater weight and greater energy. Sardinia has gained wonderfully by her alliance with France. Ail the vengeance which she had stored up for years has been sated ; all ti e ambition of a line ot ambitious monarclis has been fully gratified ; and Savoy is the debt which must he paid for ti e whole. Why should not Sardinia pay it? We recognize much truth in tho arguments used by M. Oast. Hani Fantoni It is possible that tlie Sardinian kingdom may he extended to the utmost, limits of Italy, and, instead of 1 1,000,000, may count. 15,000,000 inhabitants, and even mote. It may be that in such a case Franco would renew bet demands. "Are hon. members aware" asks the speaker, "how active the French Propaganda is "already in Liguiia and the Island of Sardinia ?" It is equally true that these outlying provinces, when once lost, can never be regained. Savoy and Nice, once goue, are gono for ever; and so it will be with any other frontier district. But we must recommend the Sardinians to be practical. It is useless to lament or to be indignant over what is done; the only thing is to be more careful for the future. When the assistance of Frauce is again to be called in, let it be understood beforehand that no slice of Italian territory is to be the price of her services. Savoy and Nice may be doubtful ground, but Getioa

p ff o ij i oil, and the island of Sardiuia are as much Italian as Florence itself. Energy and dexterity, with the aid of time, will give the Italians all they want, without the necessity of playing such a dangerous game as is involved in their recent bargain. þÿ þÿ From the New York Tribune, April 18. tiii; Japanese: embassy. We have intelligence of the arrival at San Francisco of t lie Embassadors sent from Japan, to give assurance, by their presence here, of the pet L et establishment of friendly relations between their Government and that of the United States. The telegraphic dispatch states that the Embassy consists of two Princes of the highest Japanese rank, and two others, of nearly equal emiuenee. This double delegation is strictly in accordance with the national cu»t mi. The Government of Japau is duplicate, a spiritu.l Emperor occupying the first nominal station in the land, while a temp .ral ruler, called the Tycoon, holds in his hands the real authority In their diplomatic intercourse with foreign countries, the movements of the Japanese have all b en conducted by two otli i,u Is, one representing the order of nobility established by the temporal chief, the other acting on the pa t of the more ancient order which originated with the spiritual dynasty, and possessing the right of censorship over his colleague, into whose charge, generally the principal manag in t of aff firs is confided. In addition to ih se four Princes are a number of officers of a 1 ,wer grade, interpreters and so

forth, numbering in all seventy two persons. This is the first Embassy ever sent by the Government of Japan to any Christian Power. It is true th it in the ye if 1584 two young Japanese nobles, attended by two counse lors, after a long voyage of two years and a half by way of Mac io m China, Malacca, Goa, the Cape of G >od II ipe, Li-bon, Madrid. Alicante, and Leghorn, at rived at R >me, a< unb i-sidors to Pope Gr, gory XIII. , by whom tliey were received with gr at c 'remoiiies But thev wera sent not bv the Emperor of Japan, but by the Kings of Bongo una Arimvand the Prince of Otnurti, who ruled over territories of limited extent in the neighborhood of Nagasaki, and who, together with a eon -id rahle portion of their subjects, had been converted by the Portuguese J suit mi-sionnries to the Ca'holio faith. A' this time the power of the Japanese Emperor was by no means so firmly established as at pres ii». The Japanese Islands had been found by Xavier, who first visited Japan I in 1542, divided into numerous principalities, which, though they acknowledged a nominal subordination to one Imperial head, were substantially independent, and engaged in perpetu.l wars with each other. The consolidation of the Japanese empire was first commenced by Nobunutign, a successful military usurper, w ho ruled from 1567 to 1582, and it was curried out and completed by his successor, Faxiba, who took fir.-t the title of Kambaeundono, and afterward that of Taiko-Sama. It was during the absence of the ambassadors to the Pope

that this litter prince ro-e to power; shortly after which, in 1587, lie issued an edict for tho expulsion of the Jesuit missionaries, followed up by u series of persecutions which resulted finally in the extinction of the uew religion, nnd in the closing of Japan against all Christians, the Dutch only excepted, who wviv allowed a limited trade, and to maintain for that purpose a small factory, under severe restrictions, on the little island of Desima, in the harbor of Nagasaki. Thus things remained, in spite of several attempts on the part of the Engli-h and Russians at the opening of an intercoms till , the arrival in the Bay of Yeddoof our squadron, under Commodore Perry, in 1853. The negotiations which he instituted have resulted in the cluding opening ot the that of the ptincipal ports of Japan, to in- capital itself, not only us, but to tho other principal maritime nations- The apprehensions and reserve of the Japanes , or rather of the Japanese rulers, have gradually worn away. The obstacles at first put in the way of trade have been gradually removed, and number of exchangable though commerce is much articles restricted by the small that have yet been hit upon, it appears to be gradually increasing. The selection of the United States as the first Government with which to open the most iutimate relations is more than a mete compliment

The Japanese are too shrewd a people to profer compliments without good reason. It is a fact which they are ii"t likely to forget that, of all their visitors, only the Americans have shown a proper leg.nd tor their rights and their feelings. Against the Portuguese, Dutch, English, and Russians, the Japanese have reasonable cause for complaint. All these nations have, at different times, violently interfered with their systems, and sought to break harshly through, rather than to remove, their traditional prejudices. The Japanese, too, are perfectly familiar with tlie rapid progress and the power of the United States, and are well disposed to seek their first alliance with a nation dissociated, so far as their affairs are concerned, from those European powers which they still legard with more or less distrust. This visit could not have been permitted without a complete revulsion of the Japanese policy. When, two hundred and fifty years ago, foreign©: s were swept from the country, on account of their arrogant temper, and the alleged plot of the Portuguese to overthrow the Government, laws were put in force decreeing death to any native who should leave the islands. A short time before, however, a religious mission bad been sent to Rome by a Japanese Prince ; which shows tho original policy of the Government to have been different. In order to mure effectively preset ve their seclusion, no ships were after this allowed to be built without the open stern, so that long voyages became impossible For many reasons,

some of them involving the entito machinery of the Government, an important law once proclaimed cannot be set aside, except by means so hazardous that tho high officials shrink from attempting it. And thus, during all this while, the law lias remained unaltered, and its extinction at this time must necessarily produce an eutire change in the social and political condition of the people. It seems that the most perfect freedom of intercourse with the outer world must inevitably follow. The embas-y having touched at San Francisco, Consul Harris's recommendation that large and exciting places shall be avoided until after the reception at Washington is no longer of force, and it is uncertain where the guests will first be introduced. It is, of course, proper that they should be conducted, as early as possible, to the seat of the Government. Something has been suggested as to the expediency of showing a certain deference to their customs. Such a course would not be flattering to them, nor wise in us. The Japanese will at once perceive the wide difference between the habits of this country and their own, and they have wit enough to understand it fully, ltmiy cause them a momentary thrill of amazement to find that the President does uot wear two swords, and that his visitors do not signify their presence by rapping with their foreheads upon the floor. But they ate exceedingly quick of apprehehsion, and will soon enough accommodate themselves to all circumstances. Their sojourn here ought

to be a very pleasant one. FRIDAY, 29th JUNE, 1800. þÿ þÿ VVk li ave been informed (but for tile truth of tile information we cannot vouch) that one ot t lie members of t lie Burgher Council will shortly proceed to the United States, in order to enter into an engagement witli the United þÿStates Government to lake over the recently captured Africans in that country as free laborers in this colony. We could earnestly wish that this gentleman might lie successful in his mission ; but we do not believe that the United þÿStates Government will do ought else than return these Africans to their native country. The question of the expense, which could he saved to the United States by our employment of these Africans, is not one that will weigh much with the Government. þÿ'l e li President, by late accounts, had demanded an appropriation large enough to cover this expense ; and a hill passed the Senate on tile 24th May last authorizing the President to make all future arrangements with the Coloni- ; zution Society to return to Liberia all the Africans captured. Apart from this fact, a resolution df inquiry was shortly to have been introduced in Congress regarding the belief that the Africans captured by British Cruisers are not returned to their homes, but are made to supply the labor wants of British Colonies. In the face of this inquiry, we do not think it likely that the United States would go a step vet further than the British Government and make over the Africans captured by American Cruisers

to a foreign Government. We do not suppose that these remarks will have any influence in deterring the Burgher Council from making a trial; nor do we wish that they should; but we would only caution our planters against being too sanguine of success in this enterprise.

From the New York Wcikly Herald, May 2G. Washington, May 19, I860. THE AFRICANS CAPTURED ON ISOARD THE SLAVER WILDFIRE.

The President communicated a special message to the Senate to-day, announcing the capture by the Mohawk ot the slaver Wildlire, with five hundred and seven Africans on hoard. He refers to his action in the case of the negroes from the Echo, and regrets to say that, under the mode adopted in regard to them, the expenditures will he large; but this seems to a great extent to he inevitable, without a violation ot' the laws of humanity. The expenditures on this scale for the Africans captured on hoard the Wildfire will not be less than otie hundred thousand dollars, and may considerably exceed this sum. It will not lie sufficient for Congress to limit the amount to he appropriated to the case of the Wildfire, as, probably, judging from the increased activity ofthe slave trade, and the vigilance of our cruisers, several similar captures may he made before the end of the year. An appropriation ought, therefore, to be granted large enough to cover these contingencies. The period, lie says, has arrived when it is indispensable to provide by some specific legislation for the guidance of the Executive on the subject. He suggests Congress may authorize him to enter into a general arrangement with the Colonization Society, binding them to receive on the coast of Africa, from an agent l il ere, all the captured Africans who may be delivered to him, and to maintain them for a limited period on such terms and conditions as may combine humanity toward those unfortunates with a just economy. It

would obviate the necessity of making a new bargain with every new capture, and would prevent delay and avoid the expence ot' the disposition ofthe captured. The law might then provide that in all Cases where practicable the captor shall carry the negroes directly to Africa, and deliver them to the American agent there, afterward bringing the captured vessel to the United States for adjudication. The capturing officer, in case of bringing the prize to the United States, ought to he required to land the negroes in some one or more ports, to be designated by Congress, where the prevailing health throughout the year is good, At these ports, cheap but permanent accommodations might be provided for the negroes, until they could he sent away, without incurring the expense of erect-

ing such accommodation at every port where the captor may think it expedient to enter. On the present occasion these negroes have been brought to Key West, and, according to an estimate presented by the Marshal of the Southern district of Florida, the cost of providing temporary quarters will he twenty-five hundred dollars. The aggregate expense for it single month may he twelve thousand dollars. But this is far from being the worst evil. Within a few weeks the yellow fever will prevail at Key West, a nd hence the Marshal urges their removal from their present quarters at an early day, which must he done, in any event, as soon as practicable. For these reasons the President earnestly recommends the subject to the immediate attention of Congress. He says, in conclusion, that it is truly lamentable that Great Britain and the United States should he obliged to spend such a vast amount of blood and treasure for the suppression of t he African slave trade, when the only portions of the civilized world where it is tolerated and encouraged ;ire the Spanish islands of Cuba and Porto Kico.
