Stanley, commanding t lie Wyandotte, stating that In had captured off' the Isle of Pines the hark William, under American colors, with live hundred and seventy negroes on hoard. Site had, at the time she left Conge river, seven hundred and forty four on board, there was hut one American on board, supposed to he the captain. His name is William Pres ton, of Philadelphia. He had taken them to Key West. The government will have its hands full to take care of the miserable creatures brought into our ports. Twelve hundred of them are now iit Key West, in custody of the United States Marsha), and judging from the great activity in the trade and the number of ships engaged in this inhuman traffic, government will probably have several thousand, which must he disposed of speedily.

The Japanese in a Religions Point of View. According to all accounts, the pious people in this city and elsewhere have become so profoundly exercised in their minds with regard to the members of the Japanese Embassy a> to send special missionaries to Washington with a view to the Christianization of the Envoys of the Tycoon. We are not informed as to the precise manner by which this hopeful result is to be accomplished, but we presume that orthodox means will be resorted to. A severe course of the New York Observer, followed up by a rattling fire from the American Tract Society, might accomplish the unwelcome consummation, of breaking off' our commercial relate ns with Japau, but would assuredly prevent tlte conversion of any considerable number of our 1 guests. The simple truth about the whole matter is that the Japanese þÿ we refer to the higher classes þÿ have no religious belief whatsoever. It is quite true that there are pagan temples and idols at Jtddo, Simoda and other important places in the Empire, but they are frequented by the lower classes only7. Without doubt, Japan bad at one period a recognized religious theory, hut now it is practically' extinct. Two hundred years ago and more, when the Mother Church was predominant in Europe, when monaichs trembled before the thunders of the Vatican, when ultramontanism ruled with absolute sway, a religious mission was sent fiont Europe to Japan. The missiotiaiies, it seems, were well received, and made so much progre-s

with the goveruing clas?es that a sort of semiofficial embassy was despatched to the Pope. That was the first visit of any higli official personages from Japan to a Christian country, and must be regarded as very strong testimony iu favour of the efforts of the mi.-sionaries. it would appear, however, that the governing classes of Japan subsequently discarded the religious theory inculcated by their visitors from the West, and that they now believe only in a system of moral philosophy, which, viewed in the orthodox sense, is nothing more nor less than sheer infidelity. Nor is Japan alone among the Eastern nations iu this matter. The ruling classes in China, Hindustan and Persia | have passed through the same fluctuations in religious belief, nnd have gradually approximat- ! ed the same result. Mahometanism and Paganism, springing almost from the same quarter in Asia, have lost their vitality, and can only count their proselytes among the lower classes. The next question that comes to be considered is this: Granted that Paganism is virtually dead in the East, can it be proved to us that Christianity has fared any better in the West? The establishment of the Church upon a firm foundation dates from t ho Council of Nice, filteen centuviis ago. From the fourth to the fourteenth century the priest was supreme in Europe. It was the gown and the sword, but the gown before ail and above all The Reformation gave the Chuich i s first aod heaviest blow; later came the final over'll <>,v

of Catholicity in England, and then the er.i f infidelity in France. Now all Europe is u ilitarian. There is a certain respect paid to the forms of the Established Church in England, to the usages of tho holy Catholic religion in France, Austria and Spain, and to t lie Gr, ek Church in Russia; but it is only a formal recognition of what was on e a g eat power, and has still a cottain influence over the masses The governing classes in Europe believe in nothing ideal. They stand in exactly the same position that is occupied by the Japanese. The Holy Father himself meets with small support from Catholics at home or abroad. In his present difficulty the sense of his own people is against him. Victor Emanuel takes his excommunication as quietly as he would tat his dinner ; and for the Emperor of the French, his conduct is certainly exceeding irreverent for the eldest son of the Church. Thus we have the very curious fact before us that the peoples of the Orient and of the Occident have both arrived at the same point, although by entirely different methods of pro- j ceediug, so far as religion is concerned. In tho East Christian missionaries have made but little i progress. China has a sort of evangelic d filibuster, who is still in the field, but who sei ms to | have made very little headway. The Sepoy rebellion proved that tho missionaries in Hindostan failed altogether in their efforts iu that promising field The early Japanese missionaries

8 V . & 10 I. , A; V! .1 J , succeeded in shutting out European trade from that count t y, and it was reserved for the practical. sensible representative of a young'and vigorous nation to remove the re.-ti ictions which the bigotry and prejudice of ceutuiies had thrown around Oriental commerce. The Embassy which comes to us from Japan is a puiely commeicial one. If the Commissioners shall be satisfied that it will be to the advantage of Japan to trade with the United States on fair teitns, then they will so advise their imperial master. They do not come In re to be Clnistiaiiized or converted or evangelized. When they see religious sect.- quai relling like Kilkenny cats, parsons preaching tieason from the pulpit, or anaigned in the þÿprisoner dock s for the highest crime kuown to the laws; when they understand that the cultivat'd mind of the country shifts about with cveiy wind of doctiine, and very often brings up in the haven of atheism, they may well look upon our missionaries with contempt, and urge that the finest field for missionary operations is as yet untouched. When we come to consider the fact tiiat irreligion is the order of the day, both in Euiope and Ameiica, so far as the governing classes are concerned, ihe attempt to enlighten the Japanese with the rays of Divine truth, 1 as lauglii by our piiests, is extremely impertinent. The facts that the Japanese know no Sabbath, and brought no priest in their suite, ought to be regarded as a most significant protest against the intru-ion of the Mawwurms of
the day. If the Ambassadors pray at all, it should be for delivery from the tender mercies of missionaries and aldermen. þÿ New York Herald, Nay 26.

From the St. Thomas Times, July i On Thursday morning last, about two þÿo clock, the inhabitants ot this town were suddenly awakened hy the ringing of the Fire Boll. It was not long before die situation ot tlie tire w.,s ascertained, as the Haines seem to have bur.-t forlli from die building simuliiiiieously with the tolling of the alarm, and as the I situation was high iu the hill t he eye became immediately directed to the sjiot. The building iu which the tire was burning was emirely new, and the one wo had occasion recently to anuouuce as having met with injury by the tailing ol a wall. The building being very isolated the spectators were at once inspired with the confidence that there would be no spread of the conflagration unless the wind should carry die sparks or embeis such distances as to cause them to full in among the buildings in die valley just below and ignite them. Most I >rt unately die morning was remarkably calm, and a light shower of rain just at the time the Haim s were in their greatest intensify, d me much to moderate all appieliension. The building was being repaired from tlie injuries it so recently sustained, and accoidingly unoccupied ; it is therefore not jiossible to determine with certainty from what cause the fire could have originated. We have heard many conflicting opinions, as is ever the case in fortuitous ciicumstonces, blit as all must necessarily be involved in conjecture and doubt, we feel no necessity of s tying much in regard thereto Wo have seldom noticed less

excitement during a time of lire than on ibis occasion, persons appearing to lock on with much calmness and manifesting no great desiie for exertion, as such we have in times past been accustomed to see. This, some would construe into apathy, but we are of opinion that it arose from a consciousness, with even the most slender in judgment, that there would lie no spread, and the peculiar position of the building rendered it so that it must fall an entire prey to the flames, and therefore no effort need be made to rescue it, especially as the main element, water, was much wanted. The Garrison Engine was in due course on the spot, but as we have said, its usefulness was neutralised by the insufficiency of water. And this deficiency of water draws us to the reflection, when are the members of this community to be made assured of an ample supply of that indispensable warn!, both in a time of drought and in a time of tire. We know of do question of

such serious importance to this as that of water, and none that community deservedly should occupy the eartu st and unremitting attention both of i lie Government and the Burgher Council i lorn this self-same one. It should he remembered that the Island is not a povertystricken one, that it would compare favorably in regard to receipts from taxation, dues, See', with Islands ol three and four tim> s its extent ; it ought, then, to be above the reproach that a drought of six mouths places it in such straits and that a calamity of fire, drinking to procure water, even for owing to its want, purp ses, makes tlie people ineffectual for good. Some persons, in answer to this, will poim to tlie -en, hut if it is remembered that tlie harbour is feel below the level of the town, it will at many once be seen ill it t he water is not easy of being procured unless hy means of very powerful Pumps, which we have not. The water should be more elevated than the town, making it easy of conveyance and quickly obtained; this could only be hy means of cisterns erected in the hills and corresponding to the three town Of course the outlay would ho large, valleys of tint but all valuable acquisitions are attended with considerable outlay, and we cannot expect to escape less cheap. We then say, let the question of supplying the town with water become om: engrossing tlie minds of the entiie as well as those in authority It is common to publio sc rais d in this Island annually, by means of jnild c subscriptions! sums aveiagiug about

$7.50 ), in aid of fire, flood, the widow and orphan, whose husband or parent has fallen by ihe sword, ship- wi eck, and the families ot reverend gentlemen abroad, and often the reverend geutlem. n themselves. Bui, strange as it would sen m, cliaiity rarely begins at Imme. 1 be incident is remarkable, but not less tine; we are charitable to a fault in ameliorating the vicissitudes et others, to ourselves we j>ur-ue a niggardly, parsimonious course þÿ wiio can solve þÿ the enigma? On Board the Gnat Eastern, From Southampton to New York, '> ) June 17 to June 28, I860. ) The Gnat Eastern sailed f om Southampton on tbe morning of Sunday, June 17, and arrived I off Sandy Hunk at 7.20 a. m., on the morning of the 28ih. She brings 38 passengers and i 8 guests. The voyage has been particularly fine and i full of interest. It has demonstrated the Great Eastern's superiority as a sea going v, s-el, tbe excellence and reliability of her machinery, and her unrivaled safety and remarkable comfort as a passenger steamer. As a trial of speed tbe trip has been mado under great disadvantages. Without deducting j detentions, tbe actual timo has been 1 1 days 2 hours. The highest speed attained was 14J knots, or about 16; statute miles per hour. For four days the paddle- boiler pressure was limited to 20 pounds The screw-boilers were so limited during tbe whole tiip that none of the engines were woiked with that increase of power by high steam and high expansion, for which they were designed and adapted.

The firing was bad during the fir.»t half of the rip. Besides this, the þÿship s bottom lias been so foul as to materially affect her speed. On the other hand ii must be said that the vessel was light and the seu generally smooth. The distance sailed has been 142 miles further than the shortest course from Southampton to New-York, and th re have been various detentions which will be hereafter noticed, such ns running south toj avoid ice, adjusting compass s, See No one doubts the ability of the vessel, with a proportionate load of passengers and under favorable circumstances, to make the passage in less than nine days It is a very rem likable fact that none of the engines, sciew or paddle, have been once stopped for þÿadjus ment during the whole ti ip. This voyage of the Great Eastern has, to a certain extent, demonstrated the mechanical feasibility of the schemes of her design, rs, and the economy of large ships on long routes with heavy traffic. The excessive speed expected by the public, however, was shown by the 'limes to lie impossible, without an increase of boiler power, long before tbe trial trip. Yet file all-important distinction between the size of tlie hull of ihe ship and the propor ion of her power, should precede any ra«h conclusion as to her sp ed and economy. While the lim s of tli" sl ip are perfection, and her engines exc lb tit of their kind, the vessel may he premature for the pm pose of Trans-Atlantic navigation That she is not entirely adapted to long

routes is yet lobe proved by commercial cxpeiiment. The tr.echinical experiment has been successfully accomplished þÿ One fact, however, is now beyond question the excellence of that part of the great work for which Mr. Scott Russell is responsible þÿ the hull and his paddle engines. The Times long ago defended this leading spiiit of the whole enterprise agains' the unjust attacks nt eiiem cs who, eiihe.i in ignorance or malice, prophesied all manner of failure iti his wo,k. U the result of this voyage is satisfactory to sliarehuldci s, if an examination of ihe splendid vessel proves gratifying to visitors, to Mr. Russell is due the li st and p incipal ciedit. 1 wo sets of distances run by the ship will be obs rv d on two or three days of the voyage. It seems that the longitude and disiauc po t, d on th se days in the grand saloon, and signed by the Captain, were incorrect: another log was afierwards given out to inquirers. To Capt. .John Vine Hall: þÿ Hear Sii þÿ We, the und.isigmd passengers, who have the honour of being the first to cross the Atlantic in your magnificent vessel, cannot non , at tbe conclusion of our pleasant voyage, separate without expressing our opinion of the great merits of this triumph of engineering skill and naval architecture. (for voyage, (hough fine, has yet (as is generally iho case iu Atlantic passages) been sufficiently chequered with rough weather to demonstrate that, in point of seaworthiness, the Great Eastern lias no equal in the world We are aware that the incredulity and prejudice which oppose all great undertakings when first attempted have been manifested to an almost unusual extent against this noble vessel On no point has this feeling been more strongly shown than with regard to her manageability at sea. Her conduct during the brief storm of the 18tli and 19th instant should put all such fears (if any still exist after this voyage) at rest-forever

S T, & ft 0 I A VIS, Her movements, even when the gale was strongest, weie slow and easy, and at all times so much less than tln se of tho best seagoing steamers as to be quite removed from any standard of comparison. Those who know by experience what an Atlantic passage really is will appreciate the high praise bestowed when we express our belief that the Great Eastern, in accommodation, safety and f, eedom from disturbing motiou is as much superior to ordinary vessels as she surpass, s them in magnitude and power. The supposed necessity of working her engines at a low rate of speed for some days has prevented her effecting that rapid passage which w5 are convinced she can easily accomplish. Yet, from what we have seen, we express our firm belief that the Great Eastern, in proper trim, is capable of making greater spe, d than has yet been attained at sea. That the latter will always be found equal to their duty is witnessed by the fact that dining the whole of our run from Southampton to New York they have woiked with the utmost ease and steadiness, never inquiring even a þÿmoment sstoppage for attention or adjustment of anything We fully appreciate the anxious vigilance which has been exeici-ed by your-ell and your officers in all i eluting to the safety of the ship and the general coinlort of the passengers. The Visit of Messrs. Grinnell, Minturn & Co,, the Consignees.

For the last, three days the, excitement in regaid to the arrival of the Great Eastern has been on hs keenest edge. The fact that she 1 had sailed on the 16ih inst , the same day of the depu tuie of the Europa, which brought the news in advance, together with the several premature reports of her appearance off Sandy Hook that had been circulated about, the city, had aroused the curiosity of all classes, and from the substrata of the marine districts of the metropolis to the refined circles of our wealthiest. citiz ns the one great theme was on every tongue. The offices of Messrs. Grinnell, Mintnrn & Co., the consignees, have been thronged with anxious inquiries, and the feeling of real interest that has been manifested in regird to the anticipated wonder contrasted strongly with the ephemeral curiosity which hnsmaiked the advent and movement of the Japanese. The great excitement only found its culmination yesterday morning, when, at an eaily hour, it was definitely announced that she was below at anchor, waiting for the flood tide at two o'clock to enable Tier to cross the bar Messrs. GrinDcll, Minturn & Co., immediately

made arrangements to board her, and according ly at eleven þÿo clock,accompanied' by a few hastily invited guests, consisting mainly of representatives of the press and a few of the merchants of the city, proceeded down the hay. For such an excursion a more delightful day can hardly be imagined. A glorious breeze from the southwest pi evaded, making the exchange from the sultry heat of the city to the cool air and smooth sea of the bay delightful, and the quiet conversation ef the practical gentlemen on board, together with the interesting Beetle in prospect, mad" a liip of nearly twenty five m les pass rapidly and pleasantly away THE APPEARANCE OF THE GREAT EASTERN. 01 course the principal topic of discussion was the Great Eastern, and after leaving the Nariows every eye was ou the qui sure to discover a trace of the ship. Alter months of excited expectation, continually dashed by evi r-recurriiig blunders, follies and failures on the part of the management to whose hands the great ship had been committed, the commercial n etropolis of the New World was yesterday roused to a moment of general and sincere enthusiasm, by the tidings that this leviathan of tl e deep was actually passing the bar, and gliding to her moorings at our docks as easily and giaceluliy as if she were hut nu nrdiliaiy member of the great family of steamships which have made this poit so long their Western home. We publish elsewhere in oar columns a most full and ninute account of the memorable first voyage ol this revolutionary vessel, from the pen ol a coi respondent ol the 'limes who has been familiar with the ship in her days of misadventure, and who speaks with ihc authority of a thorough and scientific acquaintance witu her powers. Ihe thousands who from every quay and wharf of the City, and fiom the decks ol the myriad vessels, ll riy boats, yachts and steamers wuicli swarmed yesterday about the maje.-tic march of the stranger, like ciuwds in Broadway ab out some giand cortege, will find iu this account the explanation nil the confirmation, too, of all that they admir. d, in the easy dignity with which this St. þÿPeter of s the sea steamed silently up the hay, wended her way thiough the mauy multitudes of our harbor craft, and rounded to her dock as if þÿ to the mauor

Its worst shafts were spent, indeed, when the coadjutor of Mr. Scott Russell, her design, r, and t lie skilful sailor who hid hoped to bring her first in triumph across the Atlantic, were so mysteriously stricken down before the hour of recompense for all their efforts and of fruition lor all their honorable aims, hud sounded. If anything cast a cloud for New Yorkers over the brilliant success which was yesterday consummated, it was the thought that neither Brunei nor Ilarrisou could reap the earthly hat Vest of the grand experiment with which their names will remain forever associated. No other cloud however rested or rests upon the scene. A Summer sea was with the ship throughout almost the whole of her passage, and a Summer sky welcomed her to Atn< rica. Favored by the winds and the waters, the Great Eastern appears before the new tribunal which is to pass upon her merits in u guise which may well propitiate her judges. One point alone of excellence, which the world had looked to see attained by this paragon of naval architecture she has failed to demonstrate her oapacity of reaching. Our correspondent sets forth with impartial clearness the various causes to which may fairly be referred the disappointment which will he

very generally felt at the performance of the great ship in respect to speed. Long since, in one of our reviews of her past achievements, we had prepared the public to expect this disappointment by showing that as compared with those steam navies of modern commerce which the Great Eastern was partly intended to drive front the seas, the monster ship was sttangely underpowered. There are vessels afloat which, with a tonnage only equal to less than one-third that of the Great Eastern, are propelled by a steam-power fully one-half as great as hers. In the most favorable circumstances this disproportion of her force to her weight must tell against J the speed of the ship, and our correspondent j puts the minimum of time in which she may be expected to cross the Atlantic at little less than nine days. Speed, however, is but one element, of success in the steam navigation of the ocean ; and it is not impossible that a quite unprecefor the rap dented Great Eastern, had the original design of speed might have been achieved of her builder been carried out to its legitimate results, without regard to the effects of the necessary expeuse upon other essential features of the enterprise. 1 hat this could not be done is involved in the simple statement of the fact that the ship was built by a company. Attempts at limitiiig expenditure and keeping alive some hope, however slight, of eventual dividends, are inevitable incidents of every joint stock undertaking. Moreover, the commercial basis on which

Scott þÿRussell magnificent s design was adopted, was the theory that a ship could be built to carry twice the cargo of vessels like the Adriatic or the Persia, with the same steam power and with no proportionate increase in the cost of working. Ihe feasibility of this theory has been completely demonstrated by the voyage of the Great Eastern, and with this demonstration another (act ol equal importance has also been established. It has bien shown beyond the possibility of a doubt that the seaworthiness, safety and comfort of a passenger ship are increased in proportion to the size of the vessel. 'I h unanimous testimony of the passenger, whose rare good fortune it was to make this ex pertinent, settles this great point Familiar, most of them, with Atlantic navigation under all its aspects, they agree in stating that never has the great sea been traversed before with such comfort, with such a sense of security, such freedom from all the small plagues and gicat perils of þÿ lile on the ocean þÿwave Such space for exercise, such facilities for repose, such guarantees against the þÿ demon ol the þÿsea as the Great Eastern affords, it would have seemed before her hold designer built her model in his brain, mere madness to dream of. This, in an age of universal movement, iu which the populations of both Continents shift hack and forth like the masses of the waters themselves, is, of itself, a victory important enough to challenge the admiring gratitude of mankind. For that

portion of mankind represented hy the stockholders of the Great Eastern another matter of interest remains unsettled even hy her Transatlantic trip, or rather has bee i settled in no favorable sense so far as her Transatlantic future is concerned. Vast as is the constant growth of Transatlantic traffic, it does not appear th it the Great Eastern is likely to command profitable occupation on a line of navigation in which her peculiar advantages may bo met and counterbalanced hy the equal speed and greater frequency of departure from either shore of her smaller rivals. It is to Australia of India, rather than to America, that the giant vessel must look for remunerative employment. Be this, however, as it may, the conception and achievement of such a scheme as the building of the Great Eastern, even if it should prove a commercial failure, must, remain a great historical success. It has removed the limits of human enterprise; prepared the way for new and vast developments in the science of navigation, nnd in a thousand ways will work for good upon the nation which has undertaken it, and the age which has seen it so triumphantly carried out.

OUR GREAT EASTERN CORRESPONDENCE. On Board thk Gfkat Eastkrn, » June 28, 1860 J The Great. Eastern was advertised to sail on Saturday tlie 16 tli of June. Workmen were engaged on her up to five þÿo clock in the afternoon of that day, and before they could lie disetnbaiked, the weather which had been stormy since noon, became thick and hazy, so that it was felt hy the pilot that it would he dangerous to attempt taking so large a vessel through ihe intricate channel of the Solent in the uncertain light of the evening. She lay, therefore, at her moorings in Southampton water till Sunday morning. About seven þÿo clock, orders were given to unshackle the mooring chains. Such is the ponderous character of these cables that it was some forty-five minutes before this could be effected. The morning was raw and gusty, with the wind blowing down the water. The tide had canted the huge vessel athwart the channel, which she appeared to half block up, but on hoisting the fere staysail she slowly paid off and got her bead pointed in the direction

she was to go. Steam was admitted into the cylinders of the paddle engines about ten minutes past eight ; shortly after the Older was given, þÿ easy ahead with the þÿscrew, and the Great Eastern steamed slowly out on her first voyage to sea. It lias been a matter of remark in all the trials, that no motion whatever is felt when the ship is under way. This was corioborated by our experience of the start this morning It was not until the objects on shore began to tecede that otic could realize the fact of the huge ship being fairly on her journey. A few þÿminutes steaming brought us abreast of Culsliot Castle, where l lie colors were dipped, in acknowledgment of a similar courtesy from the fort. With this exception our depaiture was ungreeted. The men on board the few vessels we saw- had seen so much of the big ship that she excited no emotion in their minds, and we passed without a single cheer. The ship rounded the Bell Buoy and ran into the Solent with the handiness of a yacht. As we passed Yarmouth our pri settee was acknowledged hy lowering the ensign of the Yacht Club House, a civility duly returned hy the ship. In two hours from starting we were abieast of the Needles, a little to the eastward of which we pissed a large ship on shore, that had come to giiel in trying to iuii out during the haziness of the previous evening. At twenty minutes past ten þÿo clock wo discharged our Southampton pilot, Mr. Boyer, who, on taking his departure, fraternized very cordially with his American confrere, Mr. Mtuphy. In

a few minutes we again got under way, with the screw making twenty seven revolutions per minute, and run down channel. The ship on suiting dtew twenty-two feet of water forward and twenty-six aft. Her right trim is on ail even keel, so that her condi im was rather utilii vornble to her Inst performance. She had 5,500 tons of coal in the hunkers. Being stored principally aft, this had something to do with her being down by the stem, 'l ire object in making the trip nut was not to attempt to get any great amount of speed out of the ship, hut to get machinery and men into good working order. The engines, afier every trial, have had more or less work done on them, and men wete totahy unacquainted with the work they had to perforin . One of the greatest difficulties which lias lieen felt hy the officers of the ship on all their trial trips, and now, when they started on their first voyage, was having to get under way with crew and firemen strange to their work, and then foie less likely to he efficient than if they had enjoyed the advantage of a little previous training. The experience acquired and the oiganizaiion eff cted while steaming out will enable the great ship to show a very decided improvement in her performance on the pas-age home. The lo-s of prestige occasioned hy tin: accident on tile first trial trip is the cause of so few pa-sengers crossing in her But for that there is no douht that all who could have made it at all convenient would have availed themselves of the superior comfort and accommodation

In every iustance of progressive motion of a solid iu a fluid, the displaced fluid generates waves that are sent iu the direction of the motion of the body, and propagated with a constaut velocity which is quite independent ol the velocity ot the motion of the body, aud the maguitude disposition and velocity ot these waves form very important elements iu the resistance ot the fluid to the floating body. When the velocity of the body is less than that of the floating wave, the mass of displaced fluid forms an accumulation at the bow which is constantly maintained by the continual displacement of the moving body. Into this vacancy two currents are determined in opposite directions : the latter current from the stem towards tho stern, sent backwards by the pressure of the anterior fluid, encounters near the stern a current in the opposite direction, sent forward by tho pressure of the fluid behind the vessel. Tho collision of these two currents generates what is called the stern surge, and creates that disturbance behind a ship which everybody must have observed. At velocities greater than the wave, the anterior wave disappears. I he displaced fluid, instead of being sent forward, remains heaped up on both sides ol the vessel until it has passed, and then collapses into the space which it had previously occupied. In a vessel with a full bow, the head ol water, instead ot being merely thrown aside, is also thrown upwards and forwards, aud all the pUeuom ia v h we have described as taking place when the wave of displacement is before the vessel make their appearance, and the resistance is increased considerably beyond what is necessary lor the mere passage of the vessel; lor not only all the power which is used in giving this unnecessary motion is lost to the vessel, but the bow of the ship is raised and the stem depressed, so that the line of keel is no longer horizontal, and consequently in this position the vessel presents a greater transverse section ol resistance.
